summary: Specifies the MAC layer protocol Spatial Reuse Protocol (SRP), version 2, for use with ring-based media. It was developed by Cisco. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers on a ring pass data around a circle. This describes rules for sharing the circle so that several can use different parts of it at once.

questions: what is spatial reuse in rings
subtitle: A protocol for efficiently sharing ring-based network media among multiple nodes.

tldr.problem: Ring-based network media allows multiple nodes to share bandwidth, but traditional approaches either waste capacity or create unfair access. The protocol needs to maximize efficiency while ensuring fair allocation.
tldr.mechanism: Spatial Reuse Protocol (SRP) lets nodes send unicast traffic only along the path to the destination, not the entire ring. Nodes strip their own traffic to free up bandwidth for others. A fairness algorithm monitors congestion and throttles upstream nodes that send too much data.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can simultaneously use different parts of the ring, increasing total bandwidth. Ring failures are recovered automatically through intelligent protection switching, similar to SONET networks.

today: RFC 2892 is an Informational memo, not a standards-track document. It specifies SRP version 2, a MAC layer protocol developed by Cisco for ring-based networks. The protocol remains in use in some networking deployments but has not become an Internet standard.

sections.title: What is SRP
sections.content:
The Cisco Spatial Reuse Protocol (SRP) is a MAC (Media Access Control) layer protocol designed for ring-based networks. In a ring network, nodes are connected in a circle, and data travels around the ring from one node to the next.

SRP version 2 defines how multiple nodes on a ring can fairly and efficiently share the available bandwidth. The protocol operates independently of the physical layer, so it works with SONET, SDH, ATM, point-to-point Ethernet, or other media. The ring can support up to 128 nodes and has a maximum packet size of 9216 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: On a ring network, computers pass messages around in a circle. SRP is the rule book that says how to pass them fairly and efficiently.

sections.title: Spatial Reuse and Fairness
sections.content:
SRP uses two key ideas to improve bandwidth efficiency. Spatial reuse means that when node A sends a unicast message to node C, the nodes between them (say node B) can still send their own traffic on other parts of the ring at the same time. This is possible because node C strips (removes) the message from the ring once it receives it, freeing up the ring for other use.

Fairness is enforced through two levels of access control. Global access control ensures every node gets a fair share of the total ring bandwidth. Local access control allows nodes to use extra bandwidth that is not being used by other nodes. The fairness algorithm (SRP-fa) detects congestion by monitoring the transit buffer. When a node detects congestion, it advertises its usage level to upstream nodes on the opposite ring, which then throttle their transmit rates to match.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a circular train track where each station can send packages. When station A sends a package to station C, station B can still send its own packages at the same time on a different part of the track. If a station gets too busy, it tells the station before it to slow down.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Addressing
sections.content:
SRP packets carry a 2-byte header followed by destination address, source address, protocol type, and payload (similar to Ethernet Version 2). The header contains a Time To Live (TTL) field that limits packet lifespan to 128 hops; a ring identifier bit distinguishing the inner ring (1) from the outer ring (0); a priority field with 8 levels (0 through 7); a mode field indicating the packet type (data, ATM cell, usage message, or control message); and a parity bit for error checking.

SRP supports three packet types: data packets for normal traffic; usage packets sent periodically to propagate bandwidth availability information and act as keepalives; and control packets for management messages. The protocol can also carry ATM cells (55 octets) for cell-based traffic. A 32-bit CRC protects the destination address, source address, protocol type, and payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a tiny address label at the front that says which ring it travels on, how many hops it can make, how important it is, and what kind of message it is. There is also a number at the end to check if the message got scrambled.

sections.title: Ring Operation and Protection
sections.content:
When a node receives a packet, it checks the destination address. If the packet is addressed to this node and is a unicast message, the node strips it. If not, the node forwards it to the next node (if the TTL and CRC checks pass). Nodes transmit their own data or forward data from the transit buffer, always sending high-priority packets first.

An Intelligent Protection Switching (IPS) protocol handles ring failures. When a fiber cut or node failure is detected, the nodes adjacent to the failure wrap (loop back) traffic to the opposite ring. The IPS protocol defines five request types in order of priority: Forced Switch (operator command), Signal Fail (automatic), Signal Degrade (automatic), Manual Switch (operator), and Wait to Restore (automatic recovery). The protocol applies protection hierarchy rules so that higher-priority switches take precedence, preventing oscillations.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message arrives, the node checks if it is for them. If yes, they take it off the ring. If not, they pass it along. If the ring breaks, nearby nodes loop the traffic back through the other ring to go around the damage.

sections.title: Efficiency and Scalability
sections.content:
SRP achieves high bandwidth efficiency by allowing simultaneous use of non-overlapping ring segments. Unlike token ring or FDDI, where only the token holder can send, SRP lets multiple nodes transmit as long as they do not interfere with each other. The protocol requires minimal overhead: the 2-byte SRP header is small, and no software-based station management or ring master negotiation is needed.

The fairness algorithm keeps bandwidth allocation under control even when many nodes compete. By propagating usage information upstream and adjusting transmit rates dynamically, the ring avoids congestion collapse while allowing opportunistic local use of spare capacity. The architecture is independent of the physical layer, enabling deployment over SONET, SDH, ATM, or any other point-to-point media.
sections.plainLanguage: Many computers can send at the same time as long as they send in different directions or to different neighbors. The system is smart enough to tell nodes when to slow down if too many are sending at once.
